title: perf(polars): batched sample mismatches for report generation
body:
The PR is dependent on  (#609, #610, #611) which are still in review. Keeping it as a draft until the other changes are in for me to rebase.

## Summary
Last major performance improvement I can find for now. Similar to the previous compare and stat calculations, `build_report_data` is bottlenecked by the single threaded eager materialization per column for `sample_mismatch`.
- Separated out a `_sample_mismatches_for_report` hook in `build_report_data` for Polars backend to override.
- `sample_mismatch` public method still behaves the same, but `PolarsCompare` now uses a batched `_sample_mismatches_for_report` instead for report building.
- Mismatch dfs are lazily built and collected in parallel with a single `pl.collect_all` call, then sampled individually after.

Some exciting cumulative results when all optimizations are applied (includes #609, #611). Local pytest-benchmark on `PolarsCompare` construction plus `report()`, mean ms:

| 1k × 50     |  512   | 166       | ~3.1×    |
| 1k × 100    | 885    | 209      | ~4.2×    |

title: perf(polars)!: batched columns comparisons and stats calculation
body:
Closes #608 (forgive me for the massive PR).

## Summary
- Batch Polars column equality and per-column stats into single `with_columns` / `select` passes instead of one eager materialization per column in `_intersect_compare`.
- **Breaking:** Polars comparators now take `pl.Expr` plus explicit `dtype1`/`dtype2` and return a boolean `Expr` (enables composing all match columns in one plan). Custom Polars comparators must update their `compare` signature accordingly; Pandas / Spark / Snowflake are unchanged.
    - Default comparators no longer error checks for row counts, implicitly assumes the columns are coming from a dataframe with the same number of rows.
- Docs (`comparator_usage.rst`, `CLAUDE.md`) updated for the Expr API.
- Related micro-optimizations that fit the same theme: batch join-column string normalization before the merge, and rename non-join columns in one dict rename instead of a loop.

## Performance
Local `pytest-benchmark` on `PolarsCompare` construction (no report), mean ms:
| Size × cols | `main` | this branch | ~Speedup |
|-------------|--------|-------------|----------|
| 1k × 9      | 43     | 39          | ~1.1×    |
| 1k × 50     | 107    | 55          | ~1.9×    |
| 1k × 100    | 185    | 68          | ~2.7×    |
| 100k × 9    | 76     | 78          | ~1.0×    |
| 100k × 50   | 223    | 98          | ~2.3×    |
| 100k × 100  | 378    | 119         | ~3.2×    |

Gains grow with column count, which matches removing per-column materializations.


## Breaking change (Polars custom comparators)
Before:
```python
def compare(self, col1: pl.Series, col2: pl.Series, **kwargs) -> pl.Series | None:
    ...
```
After:
```python
def compare(
    self, col1: pl.Expr, col2: pl.Expr, dtype1: pl.DataType, dtype2: pl.DataType, **kwargs
) -> pl.Expr | None:
    ...
```

Built-in `PolarsCompare` usage (join_columns, tolerances, reports, column_stats) is unchanged.


## Testing
- All relevant test cases migrated to work with `Expr` based comparison (previously depended on `pl.Series` for test inputs), behaviour and expected outcomes match with `main`.
- Added coverage for Expr return types, dtype-based dispatch, mixed temporal comparisons, custom comparator fallback, and batched max_diff statistics. 
- Removed standalone Series shape-mismatch cases that are no longer applicable to DataFrame expressions.

Ran locally: 
- `pytest --ignore=tests/test_snowflake.py --ignore-glob='tests/comparator/test_*_snowflake.py'`

title: perf(pandas): compare array-like columns without a row-wise apply
body:

title: fix: size the join-column mismatch sample by row count
body:
When every column is a join column and a join key is null in rows that exist on both sides, `report()` crashes as soon as there is a unique row, in both `PandasCompare` and `PolarsCompare`:

```python
df1 = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, None, 3], "b": ["x", "y", "z"]})
df2 = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, None], "b": ["x", "y"]})
PandasCompare(df1, df2, ["a", "b"]).report()
# ValueError: Cannot take a larger sample than population when 'replace=False'
```

Polars raises `ShapeError` for the same input. `sample_mismatch()` on a join column fails the same way, also when there are other columns.

In that branch `sample_mismatch` samples the unique rows and caps the sample size at `row_cnt - match_cnt`, which should be the number of unique rows. `match_cnt` came from `intersect_rows[column].count()`, and `count()` skips nulls, so a null key made the cap larger than the population and `sample()` raised. This uses `len(self.intersect_rows)`, the same count `_intersect_compare` uses for the column stats and that the Spark and Snowflake backends already use (`intersect_rows.count()`). Inputs without null keys give the same result as before.

Added `test_full_join_null_key_sample_mismatch` to `tests/test_pandas.py` and `tests/test_polars.py`. Both fail on main with the errors above and pass with the fix.

Checks run on Windows, Python 3.12, pandas 3.1.0, polars 2.1.0:
- `pytest` (full default run): 800 passed, 18 skipped with `PYTHONUTF8=1`; main gives 798 passed. Without `PYTHONUTF8=1`, 4 tests in `tests/cli/test_output.py` and `test_html_report_generation` fail with a cp1252 `UnicodeDecodeError` on both main and this branch.
- `ruff check` and `ruff format --check` pass. `mypy datacompy/pandas.py datacompy/polars.py` reports the same errors as on main.
- Spark and Snowflake tests were skipped (no pyspark/Java or Snowflake session here). Those backends are not changed.

title: feat!: use symmetric math.isclose() semantics for Pandas, Spark, and Snowflake numeric comparison backends
body:
Closes #602 in tandem with #601.

## What changed
- Switched to using ``math.isclose()`` semantics for the Pandas, Spark, and Snowflake backends, which matches when ``|a - b| <= max(rel_tol * max(|a|, |b|), abs_tol)``.
- Polars isn't changed because #601 already handles it. 
- Updated docstrings.
- Added unit tests.

title: feat(polars)!: use native polars is_close for PolarsNumericComparator
body:
Partially addresses #602.

## What changed

- Switch to using native polars `is_close` instead of `np.isclose`.
- To keep compatibility with older versions, will fallback to an custom expression implementation as `is_close` was only added in polars 1.32. 
- Opens up the possibility for lazy comparison support in the future.
- Updated docs.

## Caveats
- The implementation of `is_close` method is symmetric and mirrors the behavior of `math.isclose()`.
- Specifically note that this behavior is different to the asymmetric `numpy.isclose()`, which the other backends conform with.

comments.body: We could consider changing the other backends to mirror `math.isclose()` as well. As `np.isclose(a, b)` can yield a different result than `np.isclose(b, a)`, which I don't think is desirable behaviour for our use cases.

Probably worth having a discussion around if we want to switch the logic here. This would be a breaking change if I'm not mistaken. I just want to make sure we think through this properly before doing anything here.

> Probably worth having a discussion around if we want to switch the logic here. This would be a breaking change if I'm not mistaken. I just want to make sure we think through this properly before doing anything here.

Yeah it would be a breaking change in the behaviour. I think the commutativity is a desirable property for a comparison library to have. To me at least, it feels like the intuitive behaviour one would expect when comparing two dataframes. In theory it also does come at the cost of a little extra calculation, but I feel the clearer semantics are worth it. 

Open to going the other way and implementing a custom polars expression to follow `np.isclose` semantics if we feel maintaining backwards compatibility is more important here.
Gonna close this along with #603 for now, have a bigger change relating to the polars comparison backend performance I'd like to discuss first. We can circle back to this down the line.

title: fix(polars): compare all-null columns in the string comparator
body:
An all-null Polars column has the `Null` dtype, which none of the Polars comparators accept. `PolarsStringComparator` only took String, temporal and Categorical columns, so the column fell through the comparator chain to the all-`False` result in `columns_equal`. Comparing two identical frames then reported every row as unequal and `matches()` returned `False`, while `PandasCompare` matched:

```python
df = pl.DataFrame({"id": [1, 2, 3], "note": [None, None, None]})
PolarsCompare(df, df.clone(), join_columns="id").matches()  # False, 0 matching rows
```

This is the same bug as #562, which #563 fixed for all-null object columns in `PandasStringComparator`. This does the same here by treating `Null` as string-compatible, so an all-null column against a string column is now compared row by row. Pairs with numeric or temporal columns are unchanged, as in the Pandas comparator. Pairs with Categorical columns are also unchanged, since Polars does not compare Categorical against String here either.

With zero rows the same fallback built a Series of `Null` dtype whose sum is `None`, so `_intersect_compare` raised a `TypeError`. That case now works too.

Added three `PolarsStringComparator` cases and four `PolarsCompare` tests (identical columns, all-null against strings, and empty frames through `report()`). All seven fail on main.

Checks run: `pytest tests/test_polars.py tests/test_pandas.py tests/test_base.py tests/comparator tests/cli tests/test_report_snapshots.py` (755 passed with `PYTHONUTF8=1`, without it five tests fail on the Windows default encoding, also on main), `ruff check` and `ruff format --check` on the changed files, and `mypy datacompy/comparator/string.py` reports no new errors. `eq_missing` on a `Null` series also gives the same result on polars 0.20.4, 1.0.0 and 1.20.0.

title: perf(spark): compute all column statistics in one aggregation
body:
Closes #585.

## What changed

`SparkSQLCompare._intersect_compare` already batched the match counts, but it still ran a separate `count()` and then two Spark jobs per compared column, one in `calculate_max_diff` and one in `calculate_null_diff`. A 50-column compare launched over 100 extra jobs, and the cost grew linearly with width.

Now the row count and every column's match count, max diff and null diff come out of one `agg()` over `intersect_rows`. Results are read back by position, so no alias can collide with a user column. The job count of a comparison no longer depends on how many columns it compares.

`calculate_max_diff` and `calculate_null_diff` keep their signatures and are built on the same aggregate expressions (`_max_diff_agg`, `_null_diff_agg`), so each statistic is defined once. Semantics are unchanged: `TRY_CAST` to double, NaN differences ignored, arrays give 0, null diff counts rows where exactly one side is null.

I didn't add the opt-in `batch_column_stats` flag from the issue: the output is identical, so a flag would only keep a second code path alive. Happy to add one if you'd rather.

## Types TRY_CAST cannot cast to double

While writing the parity test I found that any `DATE` column makes `SparkSQLCompare` fail with `DATATYPE_MISMATCH`, because `TRY_CAST(DATE AS DOUBLE)` is rejected at analysis time (this is the error from #431/#432, still present on `main`). Per review, the same applies to `ARRAY` (including a mixed pair like `array<int>` vs `int`), `MAP`, `STRUCT`, `BINARY`, `INTERVAL` and `TIMESTAMP_NTZ`, on both Spark 3.5 and 4. Any one of them would abort the single aggregation, so if either side is one of these types the max diff is now 0 with a warning. Plain timestamps are unchanged.

## Benchmark

`benchmarks/benchmark_spark_column_stats.py` (added) times `SparkSQLCompare` construction on synthetic float columns read back from parquet, ~10% of values differing. Median of 5 runs, `local[*]` on an Apple Silicon laptop, PySpark 4.3.0:

| rows | columns | before (s / jobs) | after (s / jobs) | speedup |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1,000,000 | 10 | 3.85 / 78 | 2.82 / 36 | 1.4x |
| 1,000,000 | 50 | 19.79 / 238 | 5.22 / 36 | 3.8x |
| 200,000 | 200 | 95.48 / 838 | 12.07 / 36 | 7.9x |

The laptop was busy with other work, so wall times are noisy (the 200-column baseline ranged 45-154 s); the job counts are exact. On a cluster the per-job scheduling overhead is usually higher, but I've only measured locally. The numbers are also in `docs/source/benchmark.rst`.

## Tests

New tests in `tests/test_spark.py`:
- batched stats equal the standalone helpers for int, double (nulls), string, boolean, date and array columns
- the number of Spark jobs is the same for a 2-column and a 30-column compare (skipped under Spark Connect, which has no status tracker)
- no overlapping rows, `calculate_null_diff` on empty frames, and a full compare with DATE columns
- `calculate_max_diff` returns 0 for each uncastable type, alone and paired with a numeric column

After the review round (PySpark 4.3.0): `pytest tests/test_spark.py` 130 passed, `pytest -c pytest-ansi.ini tests/test_spark.py` 130 passed, and a Spark Connect subset of the touched tests passed; `ruff check` and `ruff format --check` are clean.

Run locally:
- `pytest tests --ignore=tests/test_snowflake.py` (PySpark 4.3.0): 962 passed, 7 skipped
- `pytest -c pytest-ansi.ini tests/test_spark.py tests/comparator`: 243 passed (the one failure on the first run was in my new test fixture, fixed and the new tests re-run under ANSI)
- `pytest -c pytest-connect.ini tests/test_spark.py tests/comparator`: 243 passed, 6 skipped
- `pytest -m spark_connect tests/test_spark_connect.py`: 9 passed
- `tests/test_spark.py tests/comparator` on PySpark 3.5.9: 240 passed, 9 skipped
- `ruff check`, `ruff format --check`; `mypy datacompy/spark.py` reports no new errors (two fewer than on `main`)

I didn't touch `SnowflakeCompare`, which has a similar per-column pattern, since I can't test against a live Snowflake account.

title: Fix NumPy scalar values in report JSON exports
body:
## Problem
The Report API documents `json.dumps(compare.build_report_data().to_dict())`, but a normal Pandas comparison raises `TypeError: Object of type int64 is not JSON serializable`. Counts such as `unequal_rows` and `unequal_values` remain NumPy scalars because `dataclasses.asdict()` does not convert them.

Reproduced on main commit `5a7a1ea`:
```python
import json
import pandas as pd
from datacompy import PandasCompare

left = pd.DataFrame({'id': [1, 2], 'val': [10, 20]})
right = pd.DataFrame({'id': [1, 2], 'val': [10, 21]})
compare = PandasCompare(left, right, join_columns='id')
json.dumps(compare.build_report_data().to_dict())
```

## Changes
- Convert NumPy integer, floating-point and Boolean scalars to Python values during `to_dict()`, including values inside nested dictionaries, lists and tuples.
- Preserve container shapes and leave the original report unchanged.
- Add Pandas/Polars public-API JSON export tests, scalar-type tests and a documentation note.

This handles numeric and Boolean scalar values produced by comparison reports. It does not add support for arbitrary complex, datetime or other user-defined objects, or change the JSON handling of non-finite floats.

## Verification
- Python 3.10.12, Pandas 2.3.3, NumPy 2.2.6: 553 passed, 10 skipped across Pandas, Polars, base, comparator, report and snapshot suites.
- Python 3.13.17, Pandas 3.1.0, NumPy 2.5.4: 68 report/snapshot tests passed.
- 14 new cases fail without this change; the Polars baseline remains passing.
- Ruff lint/format and focused mypy (`report.py --follow-imports=silent`) pass.
- Spark and Snowflake were not tested.

title: fix: only treat compared columns as match columns in all_mismatch
body:
`all_mismatch()` crashes when a column that is not compared has a name ending in `_match`. Two layouts hit it:

- a join column such as `id_match` (pandas and Polars)
- a column that only exists in `df1` or `df2`, such as an `is_match` flag (pandas)

```python
df1 = pd.DataFrame({"id": [1, 2], "amt": [1, 2], "is_match": [True, False]})
df2 = pd.DataFrame({"id": [1, 2], "amt": [1, 3]})
PandasCompare(df1, df2, "id").all_mismatch()  # KeyError: 'is_df1'

df1 = pl.DataFrame({"id_match": [1, 2], "amt": [1, 2]})
df2 = pl.DataFrame({"id_match": [1, 2], "amt": [1, 3]})
PolarsCompare(df1, df2, "id_match").all_mismatch()  # ColumnNotFoundError: "id_df1" not found
```

`matches()` and `report()` work on the same inputs, so only `all_mismatch()` is affected. Flag columns like `is_match` or `address_match` are common in record matching data, which is often what people compare with datacompy.

## Root cause

`all_mismatch()` in `datacompy/pandas.py` and `datacompy/polars.py` finds the match columns by scanning every column of `intersect_rows` for the `_match` suffix and then strips it to get the original name. `intersect_rows` is the outer join result, so it also holds the join columns (unsuffixed) and, in pandas, the columns unique to one side (also unsuffixed). Any of those ending in `_match` is mistaken for a match column, and the method then looks up `<name>_df1` / `<name>_df2`, which do not exist.

The match columns are created in `_intersect_compare()` from `intersect_columns()` minus `join_columns`, and `count_matching_rows()` already rebuilds the list that way. `all_mismatch()` was the only place inferring it from the suffix.

## Fix

`all_mismatch()` now walks `intersect_columns()`, skips the join columns, and builds `<column>_match` from each name, the same way `count_matching_rows()` does. The order of the output columns is unchanged, because `_intersect_compare()` adds the match columns in `intersect_columns()` order. Nothing else in the method changes.

Spark is not changed: with the same inputs `SparkSQLCompare.all_mismatch()` already returns the right result (checked locally on PySpark 3.5.9). Snowflake uses an upper-case `_MATCH` suffix with the same scan; I could not run it without a Snowflake session, so I left it out of this PR rather than change it untested.

## Tradeoffs and alternatives

- Checking that both `<name>_df1` and `<name>_df2` exist before using a `_match` column would also stop the crash, but it keeps guessing from names and would still pick up a user column if it happened to collide.
- Reading the list from `self.column_stats` (the `match_column` field) would also work, but it ties `all_mismatch()` to the report bookkeeping, and `count_matching_rows()` already uses `intersect_columns()`.
- Out of scope: a compared column `x` next to a user column named `x_match` still collides inside `intersect_rows` itself. That needs a different naming scheme for the generated columns and is a bigger change.

## Testing

Added `test_all_mismatch_column_name_ending_in_match` to `tests/test_pandas.py` and `tests/test_polars.py`, parametrized over the three layouts above and over `ignore_matching_cols=False/True`. On `main` 8 of the 12 cases fail (all 6 pandas cases and the 2 Polars join column cases); with this change all 12 pass.

- `pytest tests/test_pandas.py tests/test_polars.py`: 347 passed
- `pytest tests/test_pandas.py tests/test_polars.py tests/test_base.py tests/comparator tests/cli tests/test_report.py tests/test_report_snapshots.py tests/test_utility.py`: 786 passed, 10 skipped. The 34 errors are Spark comparator tests that need the `spark_session` fixture from `pytest-spark`, which I did not have installed; they do not touch these files.
- `ruff check` and `ruff format --check` pass on the changed files.

AI disclosure: I used an AI assistant to help find and write this fix. The reproduction, tests and results above were run locally.

title: fix: preserve nested report template paths
body:
Nested relative report templates can fail to load or silently select a same-named template at the root. `_resolve_template_path()` returns native backslashes on Windows, which Jinja rejects, and its extension fallbacks return only the basename, dropping the subdirectory. A folder named after a template, such as `summary/` next to `summary.j2`, also matched the exact-name check, so `render("summary")` failed instead of loading `summary.j2`.

Return forward-slash relative names for Jinja, retain the full relative path when adding or removing `.j2`, and match only files. A name that matches nothing but a folder now raises the documented `FileNotFoundError`. Relative names still resolve against datacompy's bundled `templates` directory, and exact-filename precedence and absolute-path handling remain the same. Includes continue to resolve from that template root, and parent traversal remains rejected by Jinja.

For example, `render("custom/summary/report", value=42)` now loads `datacompy/templates/custom/summary/report.j2`, even when `datacompy/templates/report.j2` also exists. Nested templates with their exact extension also work on Windows.

- Full available suite with `PYTHONUTF8=1`: 752 passed, 18 skipped, no failures.

title: fix: align report tables using Unicode character widths
body:
`fixed_width_table()` measures and pads cells with character counts. CJK characters occupy two columns, while separately stored combining accents occupy none, so report summaries do not line up.

Measure printed width with `unicodedata` from the standard library and pad by it for both left and right alignment. Wide and fullwidth characters count as two columns. Nonspacing and enclosing marks, invisible format characters such as a zero width joiner, and the vowel and final jamo of decomposed Korean syllables count as none. This also handles wide headers and empty tables. ASCII report snapshots remain identical.

This builds on the approach suggested in the issue. It checks the general category rather than `unicodedata.combining()`, because some marks, such as the Thai vowel sign SARA I and emoji variation selectors, have a combining class of 0 but still print no width.

Refs #582, item 2. This is independent of the HTML charset fix and leaves sample-row rendering with its backend formatter, pending the decision requested in item 3.

Validation:

- Thirteen new cases fail on unmodified `main`; two compatibility cases pass. Coverage includes pandas/Polars summaries, CJK, decomposed accents, decomposed Korean, fullwidth and halfwidth characters, Unicode headers and right alignment.
- With `PYTHONUTF8=1`, the full available suite gives 758 passed, 18 skipped and one failure. That path-separator assertion also fails on unmodified `main` on Windows.
- Changed-file pre-commit hooks, repository Ruff checks and formatting checks pass. Mypy on `datacompy/base.py` and `datacompy/report.py` reports the same 36 diagnostics as unmodified `main`.
- Spark/Snowflake optional dependencies are absent locally; their tests skip.

No dependency is added. Ambiguous-width characters count as one column. Terminal-specific widths and multi-character emoji sequences can differ, as documented.

## Summary

This PR implements optional batched column statistics calculation to improve performance for large-scale DataFrame comparisons.

## Related Issue

Closes #585

## Changes

- Added `batch_column_stats` parameter to `SparkSQLCompare.__init__()`
- When enabled, calculates `max_diff` and `null_diff` for all columns in a single aggregation pass
- Reduces Spark jobs from 3N to 1 for N non-join columns
- Defaults to `False` for backward compatibility

## Performance Impact

**Before (batch_column_stats=False)**:
- 50 columns = 150 separate Spark jobs (3 per column)
- Test case: ~5 minutes

**After (batch_column_stats=True)**:
- 50 columns = 1 aggregation job
- Expected: ~30 seconds (10x improvement)

The batched calculation adds `max_diff` and `null_diff` expressions to the existing aggregation that already batches match counts. This approach:

1. Reuses the cached `intersect_rows` DataFrame
2. Calculates all statistics in one `.agg()` call
3. Falls back to per-column calculation when `batch_column_stats=False`

title: fix: compare integer columns exactly when no tolerance is set
body:
## What changed

The pandas and Polars numeric comparators always go through `np.isclose`, which compares as `float64`. Integers above 2**53 lose precision there, so different values compare equal even with the default `abs_tol=0, rel_tol=0`:

```python
import polars as pl
from datacompy.polars import PolarsCompare

df1 = pl.DataFrame({"id": [1, 2], "v": [2**60, 2**60 + 1]})
df2 = pl.DataFrame({"id": [1, 2], "v": [2**60 + 1, 2**60 + 1]})
PolarsCompare(df1, df2, join_columns="id").matches()  # True, but row 1 differs
```

The same happens with `columns_equal` on both backends and with `PandasCompare`. This matters for 64-bit IDs (e.g. snowflake-style IDs around 1e18), where an exact comparison is expected.

When both columns are integers and both tolerances are 0, `PolarsNumericComparator` and `PandasNumericComparator` now compare the values exactly, with two nulls still counting as equal (pandas nullable `Int64` included). Float columns and comparisons with a tolerance go through `np.isclose` as before.

## Why

With no tolerance the comparison is meant to be exact, and the float cast makes it report matches for values that differ.

## Validation

- New tests: `test_polars_numeric_comparator_large_integers_exact` / `..._with_tolerance` and the pandas equivalents in `tests/comparator/test_numeric.py`, and `test_large_integer_columns_compared_exactly` in `tests/test_pandas.py` and `tests/test_polars.py` (`columns_equal` and `Compare`). The four exact-comparison tests fail on `main` and pass here.
- `pytest tests/comparator tests/test_pandas.py tests/test_polars.py tests/test_base.py`: 441 passed. The two failures (`test_html_report_generation`, `test_resolve_with_subdirectories`) fail the same way on `main` on my Windows machine.
- pre-commit (ruff, ruff format) passes.

Not covered here: in `PandasCompare`, when some rows exist in only one dataframe, the outer merge turns the integer columns into `float64` before the comparator runs, so those comparisons still lose precision. The Spark and Snowflake comparators also cast integers to double. I can follow up on either if you'd like.

title: fix(polars): match duplicate rows when the first column has nulls
body:
When the join columns have duplicate keys, `PolarsCompare` numbers the rows inside each key with `generate_id_within_group` and joins on that number as well. If the join columns have no nulls, the helper called `cum_count()` on `dataframe.columns[0]`, which is the first column of the frame and not necessarily a join column. `cum_count()` skips nulls, so when that column had nulls, rows sharing a key got the same number and were joined as a cross product. Comparing a frame with an identical copy could then report extra intersect rows and `matches()` returned `False`, while `PandasCompare` matched:

```python
df = pl.DataFrame({"a": [None, None, "x"], "b": [1, 1, 1], "c": [1, 2, 3]})
PolarsCompare(df, df.clone(), join_columns="b").matches()  # False, 5 intersect rows
```

#410 already switched the null branch to `join_columns[0]`. This does the same for the other branch, where the join columns are known to have no nulls, so every row is counted.

Added two `generate_id_within_group` cases where a non-join column with nulls comes first, plus two end-to-end tests with duplicate keys (one that matches, and one with a real mismatch inside the duplicates and an all-null leading column). All four fail on main.

Checks run: `pytest tests/test_polars.py tests/test_pandas.py tests/test_base.py tests/comparator tests/cli tests/test_report_snapshots.py` (the only failure is `test_resolve_with_subdirectories`, a Windows path test that also fails on main), `ruff check` and `ruff format --check` on the changed files, and `mypy datacompy/polars.py` reports no new errors.

title: fix: name the delimiter as a likely cause when join columns are missing from a CSV input
body:
Closes #553.

## What

When a CSV-family input is read with the wrong delimiter, every row collapses into a single column whose name is the whole header line. The comparison then fails on the join columns with a message that is correct but points nowhere near the cause:

$ datacompy compare --left left.csv --right right.csv --on id --backend pandas
datacompy: df1 must have all columns from join_columns: {'id'}

This adds a hint at the CLI layer, which is the only layer that knows the input was a file, what extension it had, and which delimiter was chosen. Library messages and exception types are untouched.

## Behaviour

**`--on` path** — when the side named in the error was read as CSV and collapsed to a single column whose name still contains a plausible delimiter (`,`, `\t`, `;`, `|`):

datacompy: df1 must have all columns from join_columns: {'id'}
Hint: 'left.csv' was read as CSV with delimiter ',' and collapsed to a single
column named 'id\tname\tamount'. The delimiter is probably wrong; set it with
--csv-delimiter.

The hint names only the offending side. A genuine missing column on a correctly parsed file, and a legitimate single-column CSV whose header has no delimiter character, get no hint.

**`--on-index` path** — nothing raises today; the comparison runs silently on two mangled string columns. Now a single suspicious column on either side produces a warning on stderr before the report, and the exit code still reflects the comparison result.

## How

- `ParsedInput` (new, `datacompy/cli/backends.py`): a per-side record of what `load()` did (reference, resolved format, resolved delimiter, column names) with a `looks_misparsed` predicate. `CLIBackend.describe()` builds it after a successful load and returns `None` for the snowflake backend, whose inputs are table references rather than parsed files.
- `datacompy/cli/compare.py`: `run_compare` carries the two records through; `add_delimiter_hint()` augments the `ValueError` message on the `--on` path, `warn_on_misparsed_index_join()` covers `--on-index`.
- `print_warning()` (new, `datacompy/cli/output.py`).
- Doc paragraph in `docs/source/cli.rst`.

## Tests

13 cases added to `tests/cli/test_compare.py`: the hint across `\t` / `;` / `|` on both in-memory backends, the hint naming only the offending side, no hint for a real missing column, no hint for a delimiter-free single-column CSV, and the `--on-index` stderr warning.

- `pytest tests/cli` and `pytest tests/test_pandas.py tests/test_polars.py tests/test_base.py` pass
- `ruff check`, `ruff format --check`, `pre-commit run --files ...` clean
- `mypy datacompy/cli` introduces no new errors against the baseline

title: fix: support Spark Connect sessions in SparkSQLCompare
body:
## Summary

`SparkSQLCompare` did not work against a Spark Connect session it was handed rather than one it created (issue #535). The root cause is that `pyspark.sql.functions` and `pyspark.sql.Window` only forward to the Spark Connect implementations while the process-global `SPARK_CONNECT_MODE_ENABLED` environment variable is set. A notebook runtime, a serverless runtime, or another framework that hands over an already-built Connect session does not necessarily set it, so datacompy built classic expressions against Connect DataFrames.

This branch selects the expression API from the object being operated on instead of from the global flag, and then backs that up with a Connect test session, a regression suite, and CI/tox coverage so the path stays green.

## Credit

The dispatch approach here is the one proposed by @patrickswedish in #548, and that PR is what identified the process-global flag as the real cause. This branch keeps that design and extends it:

- `is_spark_connect_object()` walks the MRO comparing module names rather than doing `isinstance` against the Connect classes, so a classic-only PySpark install never triggers the `pyspark.sql.connect` import that requires the optional `grpcio` dependency
- fixes to the non-comparator Connect breakages found while building an end-to-end Connect test run (report rendering, temp views, empty `withColumns`)
- a Spark Connect test session, a regression suite, and CI + tox coverage

Closes #535. Supersedes #548.

## Library changes

**Expression dispatch** (`datacompy/comparator/utility.py`)

- `is_spark_connect_object()`, `get_spark_functions()`, and `get_spark_window()` resolve the classic or Connect `functions` module and `Window` class from the DataFrame or Column at hand
- every call site in `datacompy/spark.py` and in the array, boolean, numeric, and string comparators resolves `F` / `Window` this way instead of importing them at module scope

**Other Connect breakages** (`datacompy/spark.py`, `datacompy/base.py`)

- `df_to_str()` checked `hasattr(df, "to_string")` before `hasattr(df, "toPandas")`. A Connect DataFrame synthesizes a Column for any unknown attribute, so the first check is always True for it and every Spark report took the pandas branch. The `toPandas` check now comes first.
- `_dataframe_merge()` registered fixed `df1` / `df2` temp views. Connect resolves views lazily, so a second comparison on the same session replaced the views an earlier plan still referred to; the names are now unique per merge, which also stops datacompy clobbering a user view called `df1` or `df2`.
- `_intersect_compare()` now guards `withColumns()` on a non-empty mapping. Connect asserts on an empty one where classic Spark treats it as a no-op; this is reached when the two frames share nothing but the join columns.
- the type check in `_validate_dataframe()` no longer imports `pyspark.sql.connect.dataframe`, for the same `grpcio` reason as above.

## Tests

- `tests/test_spark_connect.py`: end-to-end `SparkSQLCompare` coverage against a real Connect session. The session fixture clears `SPARK_CONNECT_MODE_ENABLED`, which is what makes these tests able to fail: with the flag left set, `pyspark.sql.functions` forwards to Connect on its own and the suite would pass against the unfixed library.
- `tests/comparator/test_utility_spark.py`: unit coverage for the three new helpers.
- `pytest-connect.ini` runs the existing `tests/test_spark.py` and `tests/comparator/` against a Connect session, so the fix is checked against the full existing suite rather than only the new one.

The Connect suites must each run in their own pytest process: starting a local Connect server sets `SPARK_LOCAL_REMOTE`, after which every later `SparkSession.builder.getOrCreate()` in that process returns the Connect session, so classic and Connect sessions cannot coexist in one run. The regression suite is marked `spark_connect` and deselected from the default run via `addopts`.

## CI and tooling

- `.github/workflows/test-package.yml`: the Spark matrix was a cross product where the Spark jobs are the entire cost of a run (~20 min each) and the no-Spark jobs finish in under a minute. It now covers the axes independently: Python 3.10-3.13 breadth from the four cheap basic-install jobs, pandas 2 vs 3 and Spark 3.5 vs 4 each present once, and ANSI mode plus the two Spark Connect steps on the 3.12 baseline only. The known gap (no Spark job on 3.11 or 3.13) is recorded in the file's header along with what closing it costs.
- `tox.ini` (new): mirrors that workflow job for job via `tox-conda`, so the CI matrix can be reproduced locally without a system JDK. Its header documents two traps that cost real time to find: the `openjdk>=17.0.8,<18` floor (below it, conda-forge selects a GraalVM build that silently replaces CPython with GraalPy) and `{envpython}` substituting to the string `None` in tox 3.28.
- `Makefile`: `make test`, `test-ansi`, `test-connect`, `test-connect-regression`, `test-cov`, `test-all`, plus `-no-snowflake` variants.
- `pytest.ini` / `pytest-ansi.ini` / `pytest-connect.ini`: all three now set `testpaths = tests`. Without it a bare `pytest` walks the whole repo, and a worktree checked out under the repo root contributes a second `tests/conftest.py`, which aborts the run with `ImportPathMismatchError`. The Spark driver and the Connect server are also bound to `127.0.0.1` so tests do not depend on the host's outward-facing network config.
- `pyproject.toml`: `ruff>=0.16` on the `qa` extra, since the config uses selectors that older ruff fails to parse; dropped the Python 3.14 classifier, which claimed support for a version nothing in the test matrix covers.

## Docs

- `docs/source/spark_usage.rst`: a Spark Connect section covering the handed-over-session case and the reason dispatch is per-DataFrame, plus notes on the `connect` extra, `cache_intermediates=False` on runtimes that forbid caching, and Arrow always being on the wire under Connect
- `docs/source/install.rst`: what `datacompy[spark]` installs and what a self-managed PySpark needs for Connect
- `README.md`: Spark listed as classic and Spark Connect
- `CLAUDE.md`: the testing, tox, and dispatch notes above

## Validation

CI covers this: the 3.12 Spark 4 job runs the default suite, ANSI mode, the existing Spark suite against a Connect session, and the Connect regression suite. Locally, `make test-all` runs the same set.

        ("data.csv", None, "a;b", False),
        ("data.csv", None, "a|b", False),
        ("data.csv", None, "a\tb", False),
        # ...but a repeated one is a collapsed multi-column header.
        ("data.csv", None, "a;b;c", True),
        ("data.csv", None, "a|b|c", True),
        ("data.csv", None, "a\tb\tc", True),
        # The delimiter actually used never implicates itself, however often it
        # appears (a quoted "a,b,c" survives a comma read as one column).
        ("data.csv", None, "a,b", False),
        ("data.csv", None, "a,b,c", False),
        # Two different foreign delimiters, one each, stays ambiguous -> quiet.
        ("data.csv", None, "a;b|c", False),
        # Nothing plausible in the name.
        ("data.csv", None, "id", False),
        ("data.csv", None, "amount_usd", False),
        # Read with a tab (.tsv): the mirror image.
        ("data.tsv", None, "first,last", False),
        ("data.tsv", None, "id,name,amount", True),
        ("data.tsv", None, "a;b", False),
        ("data.tsv", None, "a;b;c", True),
        ("data.tsv", None, "a\tb\tc", False),  # tab is what it was read with
        # An explicit --csv-delimiter is what "used" means, not the extension.
        ("data.csv", ";", "id,name,amount", True),
        ("data.csv", ";", "a;b;c", False),  # ';' is what it was read with
        ("data.csv", ";", "a|b", False),
        ("data.csv", ";", "a|b|c", True),
    ],
)
def test_suspect_delimiter_decision_matrix(
    frame_of, ref, csv_delimiter, column_name, warns
):
    """A single column is a misparse only when a foreign delimiter repeats.

    A plausible delimiter that appears more than once is what a collapsed
    multi-column header leaves behind. A lone occurrence is just as easily a
    genuine column name, and the delimiter the file was read with never
    implicates itself. Parametrised over both in memory backends via
    ``frame_of``.
    """
    namespace = _namespace(csv_delimiter=csv_delimiter)
    message = suspect_delimiter(ref, namespace, frame_of(column_name))
    assert (message is not None) == warns

## Summary

Add Boolean column comparison support for Polars, PySpark, and Snowflake to bring these backends to parity with the existing Pandas Boolean comparator.

## Root cause

The default comparator chains for Polars, PySpark, and Snowflake did not include dedicated Boolean handling.

As a result, Boolean columns could fall through the existing array-like, numeric, and string comparators and be reported as mismatches even when corresponding values were equal.

## Changes

- Add dedicated Boolean comparators for:
  - `PolarsBooleanComparator`
  - `SparkBooleanComparator`
  - `SnowflakeBooleanComparator`
- Export the new comparators through `datacompy.comparator`.
- Register each Boolean comparator before the numeric comparator in its backend.
- Preserve the existing numeric comparator implementations.
- Use exact, null-safe Boolean comparison semantics.
- Avoid lossy numeric casts in Spark and Snowflake.
- Add backend-specific regression tests.

## Comparison behavior

### Boolean versus Boolean

Boolean values are compared using exact, null-safe equality.

| Left | Right | Match |
|---|---|---|
| `True` | `True` | `True` |
| `False` | `False` | `True` |
| `True` | `False` | `False` |
| `None` | `None` | `True` |
| `None` | `False` | `False` |

### Boolean versus numeric

Boolean values are compared with exact numeric equivalents:

- `True` matches `1`
- `False` matches `0`
- `True` does not match `0`
- `False` does not match `1`
- aligned nulls match
- comparison works in either column order

The Spark and Snowflake implementations compare against native numeric literals rather than casting numeric columns to `double`. This preserves large integers and high-precision decimal values.

### Boolean versus unsupported types

When a Boolean column is compared with a nonnumeric, non-Boolean column, only aligned null values are considered equal.

## Backend integration

The Boolean comparators are registered before the existing numeric comparators:

```python
[
    ArrayLikeComparator(),
    BooleanComparator(),

    StringComparator(),

Fix Pandas comparisons for Boolean columns, which were previously reported as mismatches even when corresponding values were equal.

The default Pandas comparator chain did not include a comparator for Boolean dtypes. Boolean columns were therefore rejected by the existing array-like, numeric, and string comparators, causing `columns_equal()` to fall back to an all-`False` result.

- Preserve the existing behavior of `PandasNumericComparator`.
- Add regression coverage for both `columns_equal()` and `PandasCompare`.

- Native Pandas `bool`
- Nullable Pandas `boolean`
- All-null nullable Boolean columns
- Native `bool` compared with nullable `boolean`

title: release: v1.0.0
body:
## Summary

This is the `v1.0.0` general availability release of DataComPy, a major version bump from `0.19.x`. It introduces a new comparator architecture, sensitive column handling, and several quality-of-life improvements across all backends.

### Breaking Changes

- **Comparator subpackage** (`datacompy/comparator/`): New strategy-pattern architecture for column comparison logic. Numeric, string, and array comparators are now backend-specific classes (`PandasNumericComparator`, `SparkStringComparator`, etc.) rather than inline logic. Custom comparators can be injected into any backend compare class.
- **`validate_tolerance_parameter`** is now a public API (renamed from `_validate_tolerance_parameter`).
- Fugue integration removed.
- Python minimum is now 3.12 (CI/tooling); PySpark dependency split by Python version.
- Snowflake: `snowflake-snowpark-python` minimum bumped to 1.37.

### New Features

- **Sensitive column masking** across all four backends (Pandas, Polars, Spark, Snowflake) — columns can be hidden or hashed without modifying the original DataFrames.
- **Custom comparators** — pass a comparator instance per column to any backend for fully custom comparison logic.
- **`cols_with_mismatches`** method — programmatic access to the set of mismatching column names.
- **`cache_intermediates` option** for `SparkSQLCompare` — controls intermediate DataFrame caching to tune Spark job performance.
- **Pandas 3 support**.
- Per-column tolerance as a `dict` in addition to a global `float`.

### Fixes

- `SparkSQLCompare`: forbid case-sensitive join columns.
- Snowflake: `max_diff` now correctly defaults to `0` when `None`.
- Join columns `None` handling fixed.

### Other

- Jinja2 template-based report rendering.
- Copyright year updated to 2026.
- `CLAUDE.md` added.
- Dependency ranges updated across all backends.

# Summary
Commits in [489](https://github.com/capitalone/datacompy/pull/489) were absolutely cooked and it was easier to just cherrypick my changes into a new branch - reopening a new PR here. This is continuing the work from [434](https://github.com/capitalone/datacompy/pull/434) which addresses issue [409](https://github.com/capitalone/datacompy/issues/409), merged with a new branch based on the latest develop. 

## Key Changes
- Combined `sensitive_columns_df1` and `sensitive_columns_df2` into a single parameter `sensitive_columns`. 
   - Implemented as `@property` and `@sensitive_columns.setter`.
- `salt` parameter removed as it would not add any additional security to the hashing for our use cases.
- Moved hashing functionality into `_hash_sensitive_columns()` which is called after `_validate_dataframe()` and before `_compare()`. 
  - Previously in [434](https://github.com/capitalone/datacompy/pull/434), the hashing was done in the `df` setters before `_validate_dataframe()`. This could have caused issues as the column hashing was done before any checks. 
  - Changed hashing algorithm from `SHA256` to `BLAKE2b`, which is optimized for 64-bit platforms and may be more performant. 
  - Sensitive columns not found in the current dataframe are skipped.
  - Masked each column before applying the hash such that null values remain unhashed. 
- Added validation of `sensitive_columns`.

- Include warnings for the inplace modification of dataframes containing sensitive columns.
- Added/modified unit tests for the additional changes made.

## Future Enhancements
- Add support for Polars, Spark, and Snowflake
  - Polars support should be pretty easy with the only caveat being that there is a distinction between `NaN` and `null` values whereas there isn't in Pandas, I'm thinking we would simply leave both unhashed in Polars.
